When People Are 'Deaf' to Music

Understanding amusia and the puzzle of musical ability

When People Are 'Deaf' to Music

An Avazbek Reader Booster article · ~794 words · 20 target words

Music has long been considered a uniquely human concept. In fact, most psychologists agree that music is a universal human instinct. Like any ability, however, there is great variation in people's musical competence. For every brilliant pianist in the world, there are several people we refer to as 'tone deaf'. It is not simply that people with tone deafness (or 'amusia') are unable to sing in tune — they are also unable to discriminate between tones or recognise familiar melodies. Such a disorder can occur after brain damage, but recently research has focused on congenital amusia (when people are born with the condition), which is not associated with any brain damage, hearing problems, or lack of exposure to music.

According to the research of Dr Isabelle Peretz of the University of Montreal, amusia is more complicated than an inability to distinguish pitches. An amusic can distinguish between two pitches that are far apart, but cannot tell the difference between intervals smaller than a half step on the Western diatonic scale, while most people can easily distinguish differences smaller than that. When listening to melodies which have had a single note altered so that it is out of key with the rest, amusics often do not notice a problem. As would be expected, amusics perform significantly worse at singing and tapping a rhythm along with a melody than non-amusics do.

The most fascinating aspect of amusia is how specific to music it is. Because of music's close ties to language, it might be expected that a musical impairment would be caused by a language deficiency. Studies suggest, however, that language and music ability are independent of one another. People with brain damage in areas critical to language are often still able to sing, despite being unable to communicate through speech. Moreover, while amusics show deficiencies in their recognition of pitch differences in melodies, speakers of tonal languages such as Chinese do not report having any difficulty discriminating between words that differ only in their intonation. The linguistic cues inherent in speech make discrimination of meaning much easier for amusics. Amusics are also successful most of the time at detecting the mood of a melody, can identify a speaker based on their voice, and can discriminate and identify environmental sounds.

Recent work has focused on locating the part of the brain responsible for amusia. The temporal lobes, home to the primary auditory cortex, have long been considered the most likely site, since this area is most active during musical listening. Because it has been shown that there is no hearing deficit in amusia, researchers moved on to the temporal neocortex, where more sophisticated processing of musical cues was thought to take place. New studies, however, suggest that the deficits in amusics are located outside the auditory cortex altogether: brain scans of amusics show no reaction at all to differences smaller than a half step, yet when changes in tones are large, their brains overreact, showing twice as much activity on the right side of the brain as a normal brain hearing the same thing.

So what does this all mean? Looking only at the research of Peretz in the field of the neuropsychology of music, it would appear that amusia is some sort of disorder. As a student of neurobiology, however, I am skeptical. Certainly the studies by Peretz that have found significant differences between the brains of so-called amusics and normal brains are legitimate. The more important question now becomes one of normality. Every trait, from skin colour to intelligence to mood, exists on a continuum — there is a great deal of variation from one extreme to the other. Just because the vast majority of people have basic musical ability, this doesn't mean that lacking it is abnormal.

What makes an amusic worse off than a musical prodigy? Musical ability is culturally valued, and may have been a factor in survival at one point in human history, but it does not seem likely that it is still being selected for on an evolutionary scale. Darwin believed that music was adaptive as a way of finding a mate, but who needs to sing to find a partner in an age when it is possible to express emotions through a song on your phone? While the idea of amusia is interesting, it seems to be just one end of the continuum of innate musical ability. Comparing this 'disorder' to learning disorders such as a specific language impairment seems to go too far. Before amusia can be declared a disability, further research must determine whether a lack of musical ability is actually detrimental in any way. If no disadvantages can be found, then it is no more a disability than having poor fashion sense or bad handwriting.
